Republican efforts to sway the US midterm elections are intensifying with a deeply unpopular redistricting push that now has support from the Supreme Court.

This month, the United States Supreme Court delivered a ruling that empowers red states in their push to skew the November midterm elections in favour of the Republican Party.

On June 2, the court issued an unsigned order paving the way for a new congressional district map in the state of Alabama that removes a majority-Black, historically strong Democratic district in favour of a Republican one.

The decision came on the same day state election officials needed to assign districts to nearly 700,000 voters in counties affected by the new maps. The 9pm order gave election officials days, or in some cases hours, to assign voters to their new districts – a scramble that the state’s chapter of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) had called “a contrived crisis, itself birthed from political expediency”.

Civil rights advocates argue that the redrawing dilutes Black constituents’ votes as the new districting would see them represented by just one, instead of two, of the seven congressional representatives. In Alabama, as is the case across the Southern states, Black voters overwhelmingly vote for Democratic candidates. In 2024, 34 per cent of the state’s vote went to Kamala Harris, and though Donald Trump won comfortably, polls suggest he has since lost ground.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, an Obama appointee, was joined by her two liberal colleagues in her dissent. They said the decision invites “a chaotic election, held under a never-before-used Congressional map that intentionally discriminates against Black Alabamians” and “disregards both democratic values and the rule of law”.

In midterm years, the party that holds the White House typically loses seats. In 2018, two years into Trump’s first term, Democrats swung 40 seats, taking back the majority in the House. The Tea Party revolution, which gave rise to the modern populist right wing of the English-speaking West, emerged in 2010, in the first midterm election of the Obama era.

This redistricting push began as a project hatched by Donald Trump’s political team early in his second term as president. This time last year, The New York Times reported that Trump and his advisers were pressuring Republican lawmakers to draw away Democratic districts. The project began in Texas, where Republicans have strong majorities and a MAGA governor willing to champion what became five more districts favouring Republicans.

Many of these redistricting efforts assume that voters will cast their ballots in the same way in 2026. Republicans critical of this effort are publicly signalling they do not believe that will be the case.

The move prompted a backlash in California, where Governor Gavin Newsom succeeded in a ballot measure asking voters to approve a plan to redraw five districts to favour Democrats.

From there, the effort exploded. Ten states in total have shifted their maps in this push, with failed efforts in another eight. In each state, Republicans have explicitly tied their work to supporting Trump, with Tennessee senator Marsha Blackburn saying she “vowed to cement” Trump’s agenda.

Alabama’s redistricting push actually began in 2021, and as such it wasn’t unusual. Electoral boundaries are typically reassessed after each census, which is held on the turn of each decade. This one prompted a series of legal challenges, however.

The amended congressional map, originally passed by the Alabama Legislature, was rejected in a 2023 Supreme Court ruling on the basis of its discriminatory intent. On May 26, a US District Court three-judge panel – two Trump appointees and one named under the Clinton administration – found the same.

The Supreme Court’s overturning of that ruling is only the latest step in a new legal reality under the tenure of Chief Justice John Roberts, in which historic voter protections have been removed during the second Trump administration. The decision to allow Alabama’s new map was enabled by an earlier, highly consequential ruling.

In late April, Louisiana v Callais shifted the burden in cases relating to the Voting Rights Act.  The act, passed in 1965 as the legislative culmination of the civil rights movement, sought to overcome the intimidatory and restrictive practices of the Jim Crow era in the Southern states. Among its provisions was the requirement of federal approval for any redistricting changes that would affect voting. It outlawed racial gerrymandering and finally allowed the political power of Black voters to coalesce in congressional districts, ensuring they had an opportunity to elect their preferred representatives.

In 2022, a federal district court found Louisiana violated the Voting Rights Act when its post-census redrawing created only one majority-Black electoral district. But the state’s effort to create a second such district was then itself challenged, and declared a racial gerrymander by a three-judge panel.

In Louisiana v Callais, the Supreme Court upheld that decision. One of the Roberts court’s most consequential rulings, Callais places the possibility of fair representation in many districts in jeopardy by loading an additional burden on plaintiffs to prove contested redistricting efforts have discriminatory intent.

This makes it all but impossible for lower court judges to strike down congressional district maps, given no lawmakers go on the record declaring their intent to disenfranchise Black voters.

The case for partisan redistricting had already been bolstered by another Roberts court ruling in 2019. In Rucho v Common Cause, a 5-4 vote resolved courts should stay out of disputes over gerrymandering that favoured one political party over another. In his opinion, Roberts noted such activity “is nothing new”, and involving the court risked making it a part of the political process.

Indeed, it is nothing new – analysis from data journalist G. Elliott Morris suggests that for the upcoming midterm elections, the number of competitive House of Representatives seats will have dropped to just 33, from 101 in 1976.

There are now 145 million Americans living in states with congressional maps that have changed from last year – a mid-decade shift unprecedented in modern US history.  Thanks to these new maps, Republicans now expect to gain about 16 seats, which may well be enough to allow them to hold on to their narrow House majority.

However, many of these redistricting efforts assume voters will cast their ballots in the same way. Republicans critical of this effort are publicly signalling they do not believe that will be the case.

The state legislatures of both Indiana and South Carolina – two states with Republican trifectas (where the party controls the governorship as well as both parliamentary chambers) – defeated the redistricting efforts. The Republican majority leader in the South Carolina senate, Shane Massey, said killing off an opposition party was not in the best interests of democracy.

Republicans in these states are acknowledging the political reality that this redistricting effort is unpopular, even among Republican voters, only 11 per cent of whom think partisan gerrymandering should be allowed. A new YouGov/Economist poll finds 71 per cent of respondents believe states should not be allowed to conduct partisan gerrymandering of districts – a view shared by vast majorities of Democrat, Republican and independent voters.

More troubling, the same poll finds that no political group has a majority who believes this election will be conducted fairly and accurately. A CBS News poll shows 54 per cent of American voters believe this process is making congressional elections more unfair.

Republican voters are growing increasingly cynical over their own party’s efforts to manipulate the midterms to their advantage. While two Democratic-led states, California and Virginia, have successfully put to their voters new maps explicitly designed to counteract Republican efforts, no Republican state has done so.

Even with many states approaching their primary elections, the redistricting push is far from over. Republicans in Florida and Democrats in New York, Colorado, Maryland, Washington and New Jersey are considering further redistricting efforts before voters cast their ballots.

For state legislatures, and especially state-level Republicans, a new political reality is emerging in which they may need to balance short-term political benefit with the long-term consequences of their actions.

While states start considering their maps for the 2028 election, as Georgia will do later this month, we will begin to see the lasting impact of this scorched earth tactic.

Cory Alpert is a democracy researcher at the University of Melbourne and a former staffer in the Biden White House.
